utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case Number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, they're also present, I also greet Mr. Mundis, who is at the back of the courtroom. I also greet the representatives of the US government, the Defence counsel, and the accused. Mr. Registrar, could we move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'd like to ask for a point of clarification from the Prosecution. Today we have been given a copy of a witness statement which is said to have been made by the witness today, Mr. Galbraith. It's dated yesterday, the 12th of September, 2006. And just for -- just so that the record is clear on this and we are sure there is no problem, I'd like a clarification as to what time of day this witness statement was taken, since I think the record reflects that the witness was here giving evidence from 9.00 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes, happy to clarify that. The witness appeared at the Office of the Prosecutor early yesterday morning, sometime after 8.00, to provide a statement in connection with another case entirely related to this one or to the issues in this case. And that's when it was done. And out of abundant good faith and caution, since it was a new statement, it's all of three paragraphs. It's about half of a -- about half a page. We made sure that it was turned over to the Defence, but it was made prior to the time that Ambassador Galbraith was sworn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Mr. Scott for his explanation, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but I think it would be useful for the Prosecution to provide us with an explanation of the following. This morning the Prosecution, sometime after 11.00, sent a fax or faxed a document P07789. It's a Security Council Resolution dated the 3rd of February, 1994. I haven't had time to check everything, but we can't find this document in the proofing chart we have been provided with. So I think we were informed of this too late in the day to be able to deal with this document. I am not prepared to put any questions in relation to these -- in relation to this document if the Prosecution asks anything about the document today. But today was the first time we were provided with this document, and therefore we don't think this document could be used in this testimony. I am against this document being used and tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kovacic, while you were speaking, I was reading the document that I received a few seconds ago. I am quite capable, if necessary, to put questions to the witness now on the basis of this document. That's my first comment. My second comment is it's a document that comes from the Security Council. It has to do with the situation in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a situation you should be familiar with. This is something you should be familiar with. It would be incredible if you were completely ignorant of this document, so you shouldn't say that you're quite -- so surprised by this document. We've already spent is a minutes now on these matters. We must act expeditiously, so I'll give you the floor now, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And in fact -- well, first of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I trust you had a reasonably pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On this very point, Ambassador, I threw you a bit -- in recalling yesterday's proceedings and looking back through the exhibits last night, I did throw you a bit of a curve, perhaps more than once, but at least once yesterday. I was asking you a question about the relationship between the Croatian army or the HV and the Bosnian Croat armed forces, the HVO, and then I tendered a document to you thinking it was a Security Council document dealing with the presence of the HV in Bosnia; however, it was a similar Security Council document, in fact, dealing with the issue of the camps. And that was the -- what I discovered that I inadvertently, as explained to the Judge, omitted one document. So I'd like to go back and clarify that situation quickly, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P05047. If we can enlarge that just a bit, please, for the witness and the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this was the Security Council -- or a note by the President of the Security Council dated the 14th of September, 1993, that we did look at briefly yesterday. I'd like to come back to it just to make sure that we did focus on the correct document. In this document and directing your attention, please, to the second and third full paragraphs of the document. The document says: "The Security Council expresses its profound concern over recent reports that Bosnian Croats have been holding Bosnian Muslims in detention camps under deplorable conditions. The Council recalls the international revulsion and condemnation that accompanied revelations last year of the conditions under which Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were being held in Bosnian Serb detention camps." "The Council reiterates the principle that the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) must be given access to all detainees in Bosnia wherever they may be held. It notes that the ICRC has recently been given access to some detainees, but recalls with condemnation the obstacles which the Bosnian Croats have previously placed in the way of the ICRC's attempts to gain access to the camps in order to ascertain the conditions of the detained. It also notes the recent appeal addressed by the President of Croatia to the Bosnian Croats." And then makes reference to another Security Council record "(S/26419)." This is dated, sir, the 14th of September, 1993. Now, again, Mr. Ambassador, was this during the time when you and your government were raising this very issue with Tudjman and the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the last sentence of the second paragraph where it says: "A recent appeal by the President of Croatia." You had raised these very issues with the President of Croatia yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could then go on, please, to the document that I had intended to put to you as well, Exhibit P07789. If you can see that, Mr. Ambassador, I'll say for the record this is a -- also a statement by the President of the Security Council dated the 3rd of November -- excuse me, the 3rd of February, 1994, and if I can direct your attention, please, to the second and third paragraphs on the page. "The Security Council is deeply concerned that the Republic of Croatia has deployed elements of the Croatian Army (HV) along with heavy military equipment in the central and southern parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as described in an earlier Secretary-General's letter." "The Security Council strongly condemns the Republic of Croatia for this serious hostile act against a Member State of the United Nations which constitutes a violation of international law," and then continuing on -- actually I'm going to go to the next paragraph. "The Security Council demands that the Republic of Croatia withdraw forthwith all elements of the Croatian Army (HV) along with military equipment and fully respect the territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And again, sir, my question to you: Was this again an issue that you, yourself, and your government were raising with the Tudjman government?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular responses that you would get from President Tudjman or Susak or any of the other senior representatives when you raised this issue?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a hugely important issue, and this presidential statement was a major turning point in the Bosnia war and in our relations with Croatia. This statement is an ultimatum, of which the US was a co- author, to Croatia, that it had two weeks to get its troops out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, otherwise it would face sanctions and probably severe sanctions, similar to those that were on Belgrade. So I was raising this - - this was a time of crisis. I was talking frequently in this period to President Tudjman, Prime Minister Granic, and Defence Minister Susak. And the explanation was very clear: The Croatian army was in Bosnia because the Bosnian Croats were losing the Muslim-Croat war. And it was in essence a defensive effort there, and they were -- they were afraid that if they withdrew the Croatian army, then the -- our -- the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be militarily victorious and they would lose a lot of territory. So there was a real -- they were -- there was an element of desperation in Zagreb, and they faced a terrible choice between persisting with a course of action that was going to bring about sanctions or withdrawing their troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Before turning to the last topic of the examination- in-chief, Mr. Ambassador, let me just raise something based on a comment that was made by one of the Defence counsel yesterday that you were here to help the Prosecution. Let me just ask you, sir, is it correct that you testified also in the Martic case?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct that that is a case that involved primarily -- or involves primarily Croat -- what might be described as Croat victims?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that you also testified in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A case involving, is it correct, Croat victims, as well as Muslim and probably Serb victims?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, Ambassador, as you -- as the weeks of your post in Zagreb passed by, did you come to any conclusions or make any assessments about the status of the existing leadership, political and military leadership, in Herceg-Bosna and what action, if any, should be taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are starting to discuss another subject. I'd like to go back to the Security Council. I have some questions that I want to ask to clarify something. The declaration from -- of the President of the Security Council was on the 3rd of February, 1994. You said that you saw President Tudjman, you saw him the next day? The day after that? When did you see him, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage, I -- Your Honour, I cannot remember the specific date that I would have -- I saw him. What I can say is that I saw him fairly frequently in this period, and perhaps even more frequently the foreign minister and the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put this question to you because in the last paragraph on page 1, one sees that the Security Council is asking the Secretary-General of the UN to provide them with a report in two weeks' time about the advance of the withdrawal of the Croatian army and of the repatriation of the military equipment, so the time limits were very short because in two weeks' time the Secretary-General was supposed to draft a report and forward it to the Security Council. This meant that there had to be a follow-up at different levels in this matter. Two weeks later, towards the 18th of February, did you, as Ambassador, come to the conclusion that this had actually been carried out or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I can say that I met with Tudjman on or around the 17th. I gave a speech, a public speech, with a severe warning that I think rather shocked the Croatian government that evening in the Lisinski theatre in Zagreb, and then I saw him I think -- that was a Thursday, the following Monday. No, they did not withdraw their troops, but Tudjman over that weekend, from Thursday the 17th, as I recall, I don't want to be held precisely 13 years later as to the days of the week, but I think it was a Thursday to the following Monday he accepted the US proposal for a negotiation leading to an end to the Muslim-Croat war and the establishment of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. To be precise, on the Thursday he refused the idea. I went to see Granic on that weekend. Granic with -- you know, with some frustration that Tudjman had refused because I could see the disaster that was looming for Croatia. Granic understood it. We talked at length and he said, you know, Please understand, I'm going to work on Tudjman over the weekend, and he did. And the following Monday I believe it was, Ambassador Redman, who was the special peace negotiator for Bosnia and I went to see Tudjman and he accepted our proposals. So while the Croatian army did not withdraw, Croatia pursued an alternative course of action that brought the war to an end, led to the negotiation and establishment -- negotiation of the Washington Agreement by the end of February or the 1st of March, 1994, and in a very short period thereafter, the end of hostilities, if not the formation of a successful governing federation, certainly the beginnings between an alliance between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Croat authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that clarification. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for clarification of the record, I think it will be clear from context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But just now, Ambassador, you mentioned several dates such as the 17th, and for the record I take it this was the 17th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry, 17th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1994, my mistake, of course. 1994. Now, I think the question that I had just put to you, Ambassador, before the President's intervention was -- it's no longer on our screen, but as you entered into your post and had been there for some weeks, did you come to any conclusions about the status or character of the existing political and military leadership in Herceg-Bosna of the HVO, either politically and/or militarily?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I came to the conclusion that we were not going to get the results that we wanted, which were of course unimpeded access for humanitarian convoys, an end to the shelling of east Mostar, the release of detainees held in inhumane conditions, and an end to the Muslim-Croat war. We were not going to get those conditions met as long as Slobodan Praljak remained at the head of the HVO, and as long as Boban remained the president of Herceg-Bosna. And therefore, I took the decision that we would do everything we could, and of course this is a decision that was supported by Washington, to use our influence with Croatia to secure their removal from their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in general terms, can you tell the Judges what steps did you take to put this plan into action?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed this with my Croatian interlocutors, that is to say President Tudjman, Defence Minister Susak, Foreign Minister Granic. I made clear my government's skepticism that we would find that there was any progress as long as these two individuals were in the positions they were in. I think it's fair to say to say that Foreign Minister Granic shared my views of these individuals, and Defence Minister Susak, while close to them, was also aware of their serious limitations. And in the end, the Government of Croatia did secure their dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to be shown, please, Exhibit P09510. Is it correct, sir, that what's on the display now is a cable from the United States Embassy in Zagreb dated the 13th of December, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the summary of that cable and tell me that, among other things, did this report deal with the removal of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit about what was happening at this time in this regard?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some period before this, Foreign Minister Granic had asked me if possibly Mr. Boban could be given a visa for what he called an extended vacation, a long vacation, to -- and get a visa to go to the United States. That was not possible because he had been entered into our visa system as a war criminal, and so we could not grant him a visa. And so the issue was to find another country that was going to be willing to take him. And in fact, I actually had a conversation, and I believe it was at this time, with the visiting Australian minister, I think the one who was handling immigration. In any event, Australia did accommodate by providing Mr. Boban with a visa, and so he went on a long vacation. I think I remember saying to Foreign Minister Granic I hoped it was a one-way ticket, and he was removed. And after that, things began to get better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, for the record, if I can direct your attention to paragraph number 3, which in fact is under the heading: "Boban off to Australia for a couple of months." And does that again describe the situation that you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does, and you will note there that Granic says that other changes have occurred such as the replacement of virtually all the commanders of the HVO and 70 per cent of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So at the pushing of the Republic of Croatia, there had been, by this point, late November/early December 1993, a rather substantial house- cleaning, if you will?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And I think the house-cleaning, which was certainly a product of American pressure, did lead to an improved environment in -- among the Bosnian Croats, along with the ultimatum that I described a little earlier, created an environment in which Croatia was -- did accept the -- the proposed federation, and that indeed was successfully negotiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, just to finish this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Mr. Scott, I have a question or we have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, while we're on this subject of Mr. Boban's prolonged vacation, I would like a clarification. What authority relieved Mr. Boban of his functions? Was it an authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia and what was the position that Mr. Boban held when he was let go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Boban was removed by -- by order or decision of Franjo Tudjman, the president of Croatia. That is how it actually happened. As to the formal mechanism, I cannot now recall. I suppose he did, as what normally happens in these circumstances, he resigned, asked to spend more time with his family or something of that nature. But in -- the way it really worked was that President Tudjman ordered his removal, and he was removed. He was the president of the so-called Republic of Herceg- Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question myself, but I think there's another question from the Bench. But anyway, you said a moment ago in speaking about Mate Boban that he thought that he was going to the United States to begin with, and you said that with respect to the visa that wasn't possible because he was classified as a war criminal. Now, there's a series of questions that come to the legal mind. It seems to me that when a foreigner is asking for a visa for the United States, he has to fill in a request for the visa and there's a column there where the person filling it in has to say whether he was ever sentenced for anything or not. So who classified him as a war criminal? Was it an administrative decision or how did that classification of him come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour, before I answer your question. I don't know that Mr. Boban ever thought that he was going to the United States. What I know is that Foreign Minister Granic wanted me to arrange a visa for him so that he could be told he was going to the United States, but that wasn't possible. As to -- basically, the United States keeps a list of people who are deemed ineligible for entry into the United States for a variety of reasons, and I believe it was the a consular office in Zagreb that put Boban into the list of people who were ineligible because of his suspected war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I would like to ask you about the following. Previously you mentioned, but now it cannot be seen on the transcript, that rather substantial house-cleaning happened in November/December 1993, at least 1993 was mentioned there. Now, I don't know if -- if this timing, how does it correspond to the fact that the Security Council decision was taken -- rather, not a decision, but a statement by the President of the Security Council was, in a way, declared on the 3rd February, 1994. So my point is that -- that in this case the house-cleaning happened even before the statement of the President of the Security Council or also it might have been connected with some other events which we have not talked about. So I would appreciate your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the housekeeping was part of a process that was the result of pressure from the United States and other countries and so was the Security Council statement. The -- so through -- throughout this period that we've been covering from June of 1993 through to the end of February 1993 [sic], the United States was putting increasing pressure on Croatia to stop the abuses in Bosnia, stop the shelling of east Mostar, to remove the Croatian army from Bosnian territory. And so the house-cleaning that Mate Granic described was one fruit of the pressure that we were bringing to bear. Another fruit was -- another -- a part of that pressure was the Security Council ultimatum, again -- which of course was an American initiative with France and the other permanent members, France, Britain, Russia, the Chinese were not -- they went along but they were not main actors. That was another part of a concerted campaign of pressure. And ultimately, all these events, going back again to June 1993, culminated in a 180-degree change of course by President Tudjman in, you know, around the 19th of February in which he -- or 21st, that period, in which he gave up on the idea of a separate Croat republic in Bosnia and accepted the idea of a federation, moved to end the Muslim-Croat war. I don't want to suggest to you that he had a change of heart. This was a man, as you might gather from my testimony and I'm sure from the testimony of others, who went in one direction. He was -- he always wanted a Greater Croatia, but at this point he set that aside. And it -- it was the event that frankly turned the war in Croatia around, it turned the war in Bosnia around, and ultimately set the stage in about 18 months for the Dayton Peace Agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador for your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just before concluding with this particular document and moving back to some of the issues we discussed yesterday, if you look toward the bottom of the first page of the cable, there is continued discussion about the proposal -- excuse me, that the situation in the camps, including a proposal as reported by Granic, that the HVO camps would be closed "unilaterally within five days." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Next page, paragraph 5, again talks about the issue of humanitarian convoys again. If I can direct your particular attention to paragraph number 6 because you've just mentioned this a few moments ago in one of your answers. The military situation confronting the Bosnian Croats at this time. And perhaps you will see here in paragraph 6 something by Granic which is -- connects with what you were just saying a few minutes ago. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was very much the concern that the Croatians had and relates to the point that Susak told me later -- during this period of the ultimatum, that Croatia couldn't afterward to take its troops out of Bosnia because if it did the Bosnian Croat communities would be left defenceless.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms then of bringing President Tudjman to this point at around the 21st of February to accepting what became the Washington Agreement, would it be fair, sir, then to say that there were at least two dynamics at work, one was tremendous international pressure; secondly, the Bosnian Croats were losing on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in closing -- well, no, there's -- on paragraph number 8, if you could just look at that for a moment and I'll ask a question about that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the rest of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we go over to the top of the next page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you were involved in all these issues, talking with Boban, talking with the others in the Croat leadership, did you have any understanding whether they were divergences of views among the Bosnian Croats themselves?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, there was major divergence between the Bosnian Croats in had had leadership in Herzegovina on the one hand and Bosnian Croats in Central Bosnia and Sarajevo who were being betrayed, if you will, by the Herzegovinan leadership in their own area, and also tension between the leaders in Herzegovina and the Posavina Croats, who were under pressure from the Serbs. And in the end, the Posavina Croats felt very bitterly betrayed by Tudjman and by the leadership of the Herzegovinian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in paragraph 8 we see a statement from Mr. Granic about this very topic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I might add that the proposals for the federation that became the basis of the political settlement and the Washington Agreement came from Bosnian Croats who were dissatisfied with the Herzegovinian leadership and they came to see me in the embassy in Zagreb, and of course they talked to Ambassador Redman who was our negotiator. And that really is where we got the idea. It was not a proposal from the Bosniaks, it was from the Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally on the document, on the last page, paragraph number 9, further discussion of the issue of Muslim detainees, including the fact of possibly moving them to or having them transit through Croatia. And again, did that continue to be an issue during this time period?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the last sentence of this paragraph it says: "He," apparently referring to Granic, "said that the initial reaction of UNHCR to this proposal was positive." Do you have any information that you can provide to the Chamber whether you think that that assessment was rather -- was accurate or not, that is, do you think UNHCR was supportive of this proposal?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think what I can say about this is that UNHCR would not have been supportive of a proposal that would have had UNHCR facilitating the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim population out of Bosnia. Of course it would have been supportive of the idea, I believe anyhow, that detainees should be released from conditions of detention and have a, you know, a safe place to go where they can be protected and of the idea that they could -- they could have a genuine choice, a genuine option of being able to return to their homes in Bosnia. But of course that also means that the conditions in their homes would have to be such that they would be able to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, Ambassador, if we could please look at Exhibit P07475. And in particular, page 11 I believe -- yes. This is a record, sir, of a meeting in the presidential palace on the 4th of January, 1994, so around the time that we've been discussing this afternoon, late 1993/early 1994. And if you have page 11 there, going back to what you were touching on a few moments ago, I think I saw it for a moment, page 11, I think one page previous, I'm sorry. Yes. If we could enlarge about the middle half of the page, please. Thank you very much. This is Tudjman speaking, according to the record, and Tudjman says -- no, I'm sorry, just -- go back toward the top. Tudjman talking: "Did Mate Granic tell you that he spoke to Galbraith about Boban? That he told him to file a request for a visa for him so that he can travel so that we can clear our name in front of the world, although I keep on repeating and now too in the letter to Izetbegovic I shall repeat it again that Boban was a product of Serb aggression." Susak: "We have having dinner at Galbraith's place on Wednesday." Tudjman: "Then you repeat this directly, Boban might be held partly politically responsible, here is what happened to him. They knocked the bridge down, but this is war for you, and he sprang up as a result of resistance and Serb aggression and now we need him in order to make an agreement with Muslims possible so that" -- it changes to another topic. Is that an accurate reflection of the conversations you did have with Granic and what was happening at this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- it certainly is a consequence of the conversations I had with Granic and with Susak and Tudjman. But if the notion is that by having Boban travel, that Croatia clears his name because Boban -- clears its name because Boban is no longer there, then that was certainly consistent with what I meant. I don't know if he meant somehow that Boban could be explaining the Croatian position of which, of course, he would not be a very convincing person to do so. As to the other point that Boban might -- that they might somehow need him, I guess that "him" is referring to Boban to make an agreement with the Muslims, it was certainly my view that Boban gone was essential to getting an agreement with the -- with the Bosnian government. And indeed, once Boban was gone it was possible to get an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, right before that Susak says: "They're having dinner at Galbraith's place on Wednesday," which I take it that is something that ambassadors do. And then it says - and then President Tudjman, on Susak's statement then says: "And you repeat this directly. Boban might be held partly politically responsible." Do you understand that to mean Tudjman's telling Susak: When you're having dinner with Galbraith tell him: 'Boban might be held partly politically responsible.'"

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was Tudjman's message, to put the blame on Boban, which is, incidentally, where I thought the blame partially belonged. And it's an indication that Tudjman was capable of getting -- wanted me to know that he was capable of getting rid of Boban. Basically: Tell Galbraith that Boban is responsible. He knocked down the bridge and here's what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I thank you very much for your testimony and your time at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, you have concluded the examination-in-chief of this witness. Without further ado we'll move on to the Defence teams. I don't know which one of them is going to begin with the cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Praljak, are you starting or is your Defence counsel starting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, my name is Slobodan Praljak, and although I have prepared quite a lot of things here we will take them in order and we'll start with the last information you gave us where you said that for several weeks after your arrival in Zagreb you received information and realised or you scanned my psycho-physical constitution in such a way as arriving at irrefutable proof and evidence that the situation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as far as the HVO is concerned and while I was, there would not be good because I was doing bad things. Can you please now, Mr. Ambassador, tell us when it was that you received that first piece of information, when was that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information about your activities from before I arrived in Croatia as ambassador. After all, in preparing to take up my post, I received a whole series of briefings and I talked to people. And what I testified to was not that I received some particular -- one particular piece of information, but that I came to the conclusion that as long as you and Boban were in the positions that you had, we would not be able to end the atrocities which were being committed by the HVO in Bosnia, and that therefore it was essential for Boban and you to be removed. And my government set out to do what we could to make that happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you spoke at length and gave lengthy answers to the Prosecutor, Mr. Scott. I understand your eloquence, that it is great, and that you can repeat everything each and every time. However, I would like to ask you on this occasion, within the frameworks of the right granted me here, to tell me who, when, on the basis of what you arrived at that information about me. Now, information and knowledge of somebody begins either when you see that person, when you hear about him, or through some other perception -- organ of perception or from somebody else, that is to say, based on circumstances, that the man was there, that he said such and such, that he did such and such, or failed to do such and such. So can you now give me an example, any example whatsoever that states that Slobodan Praljak on such and such an occasion did such and such thing wrong, failed to do the right thing, or uttered something which went against the grain of any positive law?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the risk of repeating myself, you were the commander of the HVO. The HVO refused to permit humanitarian convoys access to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The HVO shelled into -- fired shells into east Mostar doing great damage, killing large numbers of people. The HVO destroyed some of the historic monuments, including probably the most famous historic monument in former Yugoslavia, the old bridge in Mostar. The HVO held large numbers of prisoners in inhumane conditions. The HVO used those prisoners as -- in forced labour, in violation of international law. Rapes took place in HVO-run camps. And you were in charge of this. And when we asked that this stop, when we made the strongest possible demarches to the Government of Croatia, which we considered responsible, and they said that they were raising this with you, basically the problem was not corrected. So I took -- took the view --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I took the view that you needed to go and so did Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately, I still have not received any intonations about all this. Here we have the Honourable Trial Chamber and everybody else saw precisely the following, that Slobodan Praljak, through his own authority, let through both convoys into Mostar, not Granic who held speeches over there. So I'd like to ask you to answer the following question in that regard. In conducting research and into seeing how we can come at the conclusion of who is responsible for what - and I don't question or challenge your sources of information - I did my own research and found that in the United States of America, for instance, every year there are 25 million registered crimes. Of that number, intentional killing amounts to 14.276; intentional killing through fire-arms, violent crimes, 900.000; 2 million rapes, and so on and so forth. Those are various. Now, following on from that same logic, that somebody has to be guilty and be blamed and the United States of America are a civilised, organised, wealthy state, can you believe me when I say that I would have given this same speech on the opposite side and said: You have to replace such and such a person in power or this authority because more than 14 per cent of the crimes that take place in the world take place in the United States and the situation is similar in other countries. So do you at least share my opinion in part about that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm not sure what the question is. I've heard a long statement, but is there a specific question that's been put to the Ambassador, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was indeed a very long one, but on the basis of what I was able to understand, Mr. Praljak seems to be saying that you had information according to which he himself and Boban for responsible for a series of facts that you listed. Now the accused wishes to know what you base that on, and to quote -- he quoted an example that with respect to humanitarian convoys - and we had a proof of evidence at least once and we saw this, had evidence of this - that at least once he was responsible for allowing the humanitarian convoy to enter Mostar. Now what he seems to be saying is this: In view of the number of crimes that could have been committed and were committed, what allows you to assert that he is to blame or he is responsible? So the question was a long one and I tried to summarise it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood the question, Your Honour. Obviously I see no connection between the terrible crime rate in the United States and the situation in Bosnia. We expected convoys to go into Bosnia every single day. We expected convoys to go into Mostar every single day, and they were obstructed practically every single day by the HVO. And this was not a group of rogue soldiers; this was a command decision by the HVO. And when we finally brought enough pressure to bear through Croatia, in fact the convoys went through. We -- the shooting into east Mostar was not some private individual shooting off -- shooting off --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to answer the question. The shooting into east Mostar was by artillery. This was by an organised military force that was shooting into civilian areas, destroying an ancient cultural heritage, killing people. The camps were not some kidnapping of an individual held in a basement, it was the holding of thousands of people in organised, military-run camps in inhumane conditions. The organised labour patrols was not some individual taken out with a gun to dig trenches but organised work parties. These, in short, were the acts of an organised authority of which Mr. Boban was the political chief and Mr. Praljak was the military chief, and that is why I held him responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, by the words you used, you neither proved that the HVO was a military wing, nor do you have any facts according to which any order was issued ever to ban any convoy from entering. And in fact, witnesses have shown that it was not necessary for 360 tons to be brought into Mostar every day. And after this convoy was let through, convoys entered Mostar on a regular basis, and I don't have to say who was responsible for that. We're going to discuss that at this Tribunal for the next two years. May I have 3D00141 on e-court, please, may I have that exhibit on e-court. Mr. Ambassador, on the 1st of September, and that was far before the United Nations exerted any pressure and before you brought any pressure to bear against Franjo Tudjman, and before the United States of America did so, Slobodan Praljak allowed the entrance of a television crew from Germany to enter the Gabela prison led my Mira Ivanisevic. Suffice it to say that I did not have any -- or that I used my authority and the television crew filmed what they found there and that was broadcast in the world, and it was only after that that knowledge of this went through and justified reactions. However, on the 1st of September, I allowed the television crew of the CDF to enter and then a journalist from the Globus magazines and others, they testified about this, some material was shown and some wasn't, but information of what was going on there did seep through thanks to my own intervention and it was only then when that the truth came to be known and that is when you, Mr. Ambassador, reacted in the best way you thought possible. I'd now like to have the next exhibit shown -- or rather, let me first ask you if you understood what I've been saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, would you like to ask the Ambassador a question on the basis of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Mr. Galbraith, can you imagine a situation where someone is really in command and then allowing -- doing evil things and then allow a television crew to come in and film it all unless he was somebody who was deranged? Do you think some -- that can only be done by somebody who is deranged or does it speak about something else, something that might be quite opposite to your opinions of me, for instance?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated the 1st of September, 1993. As I have testified for much of yesterday and today, my own interventions with President Tudjman began on the day I presented my credentials, which was the 28th of June, 1993. On the 6th of July, 1993, we threatened Croatia with sanctions because of the conduct of the HVO. You will recall that around the 20th of August I called President Tudjman in Brioni to warn him in the most severe terms of the consequences for Croatia of not stopping the atrocities for which we -- of the HVO for which we held Croatia responsible. And of course this was a constant theme of my meetings with Tudjman, Granic, and Susak in July and August. One of our demands, as I've testified, is that the -- is that there be access to the camps by international representatives, by foreign embassies, and indeed we had access to the camps because of our pressure in July, and by the press. So I am not at all surprised that as a result of international pressure, serious international pressure exerted on -- including threat of sanctions, exerted on Croatia that Mr. Praljak should have been forced to issue a statement of this kind on the 1st of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witnesses who came here claim that this was on the 6th of September. You said that on the 24th of July a convoy was released through and then on the 21st one was allowed to pass through even without your intervention. We were able to see that here with another witness. When do you think I became the chief of Main Staff? Do you know on what date that was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this stage I do not remember, but perhaps you could tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I could, but isn't it peculiar that you have a very clear opinion about me without knowing when I took the office. Don't you think that you should know that? Please don't talk -- or please don't look at the Prosecutor. My question is: How is it possible -- you're an American, an educated man, how is it possible for you to speak about somebody being responsible without knowing when he incurred that responsibility -- or rather, when he took the office? Thank you. On the 24th of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hold on a second. If Mr. Praljak is going to put a question to the witness, then let the witness answer as best he's able. No one is going to expect everyone to recall every detail and date, but if Mr. Praljak is going to put questions, let the witness answer, number one. Number two, I submit that Mr. Praljak has mischaracterised the record. The testimonies about -- excuse me, the testimony about convoys getting into Mostar was at the end of August, not the end of July, as reflected in Exhibit P09506, August, end of August, not July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I took over that position in late July, on the 24th of July. Based on the documents provided by Mr. Galbraith, it was clear that at that period of time, Bugojno fell and that Gornji Vakuf and Rama were at risk. On the basis of that, it was necessary to establish what I did between the 24th and the 28th, what I did and where. However, it seems that Mr. Galbraith believed it unnecessary to be established. Thus can we please put on the ELMO a document --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope I can respond to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, please. [Interpretation] Please answer. Please tell me -- or rather, let me expand my question. I was commander for six and a half months near Sunja near Susak, and then I became assistant defence minister, and then I was commander of the south-east part of Herzegovina when Mostar was liberated in the Neretva valley. We will get to the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, if we're going to have this information stated to Mr. Galbraith, can we have the dates for these periods, please. I was commander for six and a half months. When? And I became assistant defence minister. When? If we're going to have the information, let's get all the information, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness has made some allegations, and obviously he said he was briefed before he came into the country as Ambassador. Now, it's up to the Ambassador to tell us those particular dates, if he knows. If he doesn't knows, that's fine. If he knew them back then and doesn't remember today, I can see his memory being jogged, but I think we need to go step by step, and at this point in time I think it's very crucial because obviously it appears from his testimony that he had already formed an opinion before he arrived based on information that he was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ambassador, Mr. Praljak says that he was appointed in July. He says he was appointed on the 24th of July, and we heard it that this was a period in which Bugojno fell. Were you aware of the fact that an ABiH offensive had been launched as a result of which there was troop movement and the movement of refugees in the field? And do you know that at that point in time Mr. Praljak was appointed to the position in question? That was on the 24th of July. I understand that you're being asked a question about something that happened over ten years ago. Perhaps you can't remember. In that case, say you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, I don't remember the specific dates. But I -- what I can say is that the United States, as I've testified with great specificity, partly because I have the cables that were sent at the time, the United States was putting pressure on Croatia from the 28th of June, from the date of my arrival, and I cited specific instances of the pressure that we would have put on Croatia. As to the atrocities that we were concerned about, these were continuing and, indeed, intensifying through the summer of 1993, including in the period after Mr. Praljak says that he was appointed the HVO commander. And I stand by my statement that I came to the conclusion - he may feel that my conclusion was wrong, but it certainly was my conclusion - that he had to go. And indeed he went, and he went because of US pressure -- or certainly because -- at least I can say that US pressure contributed to his departure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Naturally that is not true, Mr. Galbraith. I left of my own free will. I don't know what pressure United States applied, but now that you're mentioning the United States I have to tell you I'm not impressed. And whenever you are strapped for arguments you bring up the United States. I'm really not impressed. For example, when the embargo was introduced, and I will go back to that, two nations were left defenceless at the face of ruthless Serbian power. So I don't really expect you to support your claims with any firm arguments, that is your conclusion. I have not heard you bring up anything that would be useful to this Bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you are testifying now. What you have to do is put questions to the witness and use documents to support the questions that you ask.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please put a document on the ELMO, and we'll take it from there. Is it on the ELMO yet? This document. Can you please scroll down. The heading is always the same: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Galbraith, will you please read this document.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatian community Herceg- Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, Main Staff number 02-2/1-01-2338/93 IZM forward command post Citluk, 5th September, 1993/handwritten approved/. Demand by the transfer of helicopter OS HRZ Zagreb. We ask you to accomplish the transfer of the heavy wounded Almira Candzic /handwritten doctor/, born in 194/illegible/dg. Status post amputatione numeri dex. Vulus explozivus abdeninis." "For the heavy degree of the wound, it is necessary to transfer her from Mostar (Mostarsko blato) KBC Zagreb /handwritten Split illegible/. "Respectfully yours." "Commander of the GS HVO." "General Major Slobodan Praljak (signed and stamped)."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know -- you've spent quite some time in the region. Do you know whether Almira Candzic, can you tell or will you take my word for it that she is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is a good indication, and I'll take your word for it. If I might add, because I didn't want your last speech to go unanswered, when I speak about the United States, of course I was there in my capacity as the American ambassador and therefore not as an individual but representing my country. But on the question of the arms embargo, I have to say that I agree with you and my government -- at least the Clinton administration agreed with you that it was a terribly wrong decision to impose an embargo to have the aggressor have the arms and to have left defenceless Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, and as you know, we took the decision that we would not enforce that embargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. Thank you for your answer. However, I know that that is what the situation was, and I have difficulty accepting it as a mistake. One can make a mistake when designing clothes or something like that. This is what you used as an excuse, namely Mr. Clinton and Mr. Holbrooke. This was the greatest case of loss of collective security since the times of Hitler. So this was no mistake. All consequences that ensued following such an attitude are very hard to calculate, and I'm not talking only about human casualties, but also the destruction of property and the destruction of society. So can you tell me, looking at the sociological factors how such an act contributed to the destruction of moral tissue of both the Muslim and Croatian nations?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just to -- for the record, the arms embargo was imposed in 1991 by the previous American administration. President Clinton made clear that he did not support the arms embargo. We sought to have it repealed, but we could not get the P5, each of whom had a veto, to repeal it. But as Richard Holbrooke said and certainly something that I said during my time in Zagreb, we did see the conflict in Bosnia as the greatest failure of collective security since the Second World War, since the period leading up to the Second World War. It was a tragedy. I am -- I think -- I am very proud of the role my country played and American diplomacy played, in bringing that conflict to an end, beginning with the end of the Muslim- Croat war in 1994 and the Washington Agreement. Now that I'm a private citizen I guess I can say this bluntly. I wish we did what we did in 1995 much sooner, but I'm glad that we did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have to have our 20- minute technical break now, which means that we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the registry to put 3D00375 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: This is a letter sent to Madam Duska Lastric-Djuric personally to the general consular office of the United States at the time when Colonel Herrick came to visit me for the first time as an envoy of the Ministry of Defence. It was naturally proved for the colonel to tour Ploce, the port in Zadar and Split in order to establish to what extent it was possible to deliver the humanitarian aid from the United States. Do you see that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know Richard Herrick and do you know that following this he was the US military attache for many years in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 3D0037?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: In this letter I, as my capacity as assistant defence minister, I approve the passage of Mr. Richard Herrick, and I give him the approval to see all the things that he was interested in. And I assigned to him Goran Pavelic to escort him on this trip to Split and Ploce. Is this correct? Is that stated there, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see 3D00736? This is the reply of Colonel Richard Herrick where he thanks for all the assistance provided to him, the organisation, the meetings were very successful. Mr. Pavelic was of great assistance. Everything was carried out very successfully, and once again thanks us. Is that what is stated in the response?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does thank you for your remarkable help and organisation on his trip, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Herrick came quite a long time prior to you. I think that there was another gentleman, Mr. Serelis [phoen] there as well. You came at the time when the war was already waging in Croatia for two years and two months. Were you informed about other relations and other contacts I had with Mr. Herrick personally and people who were then working in the consul general's office of the United States? Did you receive such information?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Are you aware -- I hope you won't mind me asking you something personal. If I'm not mistaken, I heard your name for the first time in relation to your acts aimed at advocating the interests of the Kurds back when Saddam Hussein tried to poison them with chemical weapons. Is that true and are you one of the few people in the world involved in it, in writing about it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did write about it in the 1980s, and in fact it's the subject of my book published this year "The End of Iraq."

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you kindly. That means that I was not mistaken. I think that I saw the photographs and I saw your name mentioned either in Stern or Der Spigel, one of those magazines. So let me go back to my question. Do you know that members -- rather, representatives of the military office of the United States and I, that is to say Mr. Herrick and I, immediately following the liberation of Mostar worked a great deal together to investigate whether in the factory in Bijelo Polje near Mostar, yperite was manufactured for the JNA. General Binenfeld took active participation in it. Did you ever hear of this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I know what you're talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that yperite is mustard gas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, mustard gas. I do know what you're talking about, but I fear that this line of questioning goes outside the scope of that which I'm allowed to testify about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Herrick, Colonel Herrick, and Mr. Sarac, whose rank escapes me right now. I don't know whether he's a colonel --

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether during the time while I was the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO from the 24th of July until the 8th of November, 1993, they toured the positions as they found appropriate when they wanted, where they wanted, and what they wanted as far as the military component was concerned. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that Colonel Herrick and Mr. Sarac had access to -- had extremely good access to the Croatian military and to the -- and to the HVO, and I'm aware that the -- that the Bosnian Croat leadership provided access to the defence attache's team and to our diplomats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear from them or from any other journalist that during the time while I was in command there was a ban on visiting any location at any time in order to see everything that needed to be seen? Did you ever hear that I banned something like that, that I banned anyone visiting any place?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly do not recall hearing that you had banned any visits. I -- members of the international community, the International Committee of the Red Cross, for example, UNPROFOR, journalists other embassies did have enormous difficulty in gaining access to places, including prison camps, and even when US embassy team went into prison camps - and I would be the first to say that the US embassy had special access because of our relationship with Croatia - but even when they went into the prison camps -- prison camp at Rodoc, the Heliodrom, they were denied the opportunity to conduct interviews with the prisoners in private, which of course is essential to understanding what's going on there. The commander wouldn't say his name, and so there were restrictions on what they could do that significantly limited their ability to get the -- get to the facts, even though they had been allowed access.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I'm not even trying to challenge your information or deny it. All I can do is ask you whether you are familiar with the structure of the HVO, which would be a necessary prerequisite in order to establish somebody's responsibility. Are you familiar with the structure of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly was familiar with it at the time that I was dealing with this issue. I think I retain a -- perhaps a general familiarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to point out, since we can't discuss this subject - and I do understand the reasons for which a serious country who protects its natural interests - but I do have a list of another 15 joint actions, none of which have been referred to here, joint actions -- actions conducted with Mr. Herrick and others, with others from that part of the US embassy. But you read some things written -- you read the book "My Life" written by President Bill Clinton?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I have not read the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the broad picture again, what happened in our territory was -- on a smaller scale. I'd like to read out a few passages from this book and I'd like you to confirm whether this is how events, in fact, unfolded. Yes, thank you. Now he's referring to Slobodan Milosevic. He says he then staged an event and made it seem as if he was withdrawing his army from Bosnia, whereas arms, supplies, and the Bosnian Serbs were left under the control of the commander Ratko Mladic. The fighting and the killing continued in the course of the year 1992. The leaders of the European community acted in a reserved manner, and Bush's government was unsure as to how they should act. And they were not willing to confront new problems in a year when elections were to be held. So this problem was left for the European Community to deal with. However, Bush's government did request that the UN impose economic sanctions on Serbia. Boutros Boutros-Ghali was against this at the beginning, as well as the French, the English, et cetera, et cetera. Are you familiar with such events before you arrived on the stage over there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, two objections. Number one, I object to the relevance entirely of this -- to this case. None of these matters have the slightest connection to this case, therefore completely irrelevant. Number two, at least by my understanding, I think this goes outside of the scope of the testimony that the United States government had agreed to allow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you know that you can only ask questions that directly relate to the questions that the Prosecution put to the witness. In what way is this question related to a question put to the witness and to a question answered? Since an objection has been raised, so how does this question relate to a reply provided by the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is of extreme importance to understand all these matters. We are trying to use a reductionist model and to reduce all these events and attribute them to a rough form of determinism that has no basis in reality, that doesn't correspond to the way in which one should understand the broader picture, the way in which one should understand the embargo that was enforced, the pressure brought to bear, the lobbying engaged in, the numerous conferences that were held. All these factors had an influence on the events and resulted in the death of a small nation. Now there are some rapid conclusions that have been drawn by the Ambassador. For example, everything is being concept aside and an incredible logic is appealed to, to demonstrate that crimes were committed, that Praljak was commander of the Main Staff. I'm not quite sure how things were structured or organised, but he is guilty. Your Honour, if we fail to understand what Bill Clinton has honestly put down on paper with regard to the embargo and the way in which certain countries obstructed peace, the way in which the war was prolonged, it will be impossible for us to understand the turmoil of war, the folly of the population, of the people who were panicking because their fear, their hunger, and we won't be able to understand the nature of the people who were supposed to be held to account for such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said -- you mentioned the question that Mr. Praljak put and said it should be related to the previous question, but this is a new subject and perhaps it wasn't quite clear. He's moving on to a new subject now as to the link to the testimony of this witness's concerned -- well, my submission would be that Mr. Galbraith's testimony commences from the time that he arrived in Croatia, from the time that he assumed his post in the embassy. This film started a long time ago, at least as early as the declaration of independence in Slovenia and Croatia and then of other republics. So certain introductory remarks, certain circumstances are important for us to understand the actual weight or value of the facts that the witness has been testifying about here. But as of July 1993, the film started two years prior to that date and then it continued when the Ambassador assumed his position. But I think that this is relevant and it's within the scope. This is the first part of the film that Mr. Praljak wants to put questions about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case it would have been more appropriate to ask the Ambassador, to ask him to respond to a question about the political situation, to -- he discovered when he assumed his position. And then you could have presented the witness with this passage from the book and you could have asked him to confirm or to refute the passage. It's a matter of technique when questioning a witness. Ambassador, the accused has read a passage from a book and the passage concerns the situation in 1991, 1992, and 1993. By citing this passage he would like you to confirm certain facts or to refute them, to deny them. What would be interesting from a legal point of view is to know that when you assumed your position were you familiar with the overall situation in the former Yugoslavia, were you familiar with the problems that concerned Slovenia, were you familiar with Slobodan Milosevic's actions, were you familiar with all these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I travelled to the former Yugoslavia four times starting in December of 1991 and three times in 1992, so I did have a first-hand familiarity. I met with the leaders of all the republics -- or all the states that emerged and also Mr. Rugova in Kosovo, went to Dubrovnik -- my first visit to Dubrovnik was just a few days after the horrific shelling of the city on St. Nikolas day. I was there December 18th, 1991, and they had actually to arrange a cease-fire since I came from Montenegro up there. So I had a first-hand experience with the situation there, and as I indicated in my previous answer, naturally I also received a lot of briefings as I prepared to -- and talked to people as I prepared for my -- my new assignment. It's a little hard for me to comment on the passage from President Clinton's part, in part because I don't have it before me and in part because things are always hard if they're read from the Croatian translation back to English. And I know that this is a little outside the scope, but these are very broad -- broad issues. I certainly can say that what President Clinton described is -- would conform with my general understanding, that is to say, that in 1992 -- and now I forget the date although I wrote about it, actually, in a report that I did called the "Ethnic cleansing of Bosnia and Herzegovina," Milosevic withdrew, supposedly, the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina, leaving behind the -- the Serb soldiers from Bosnia who simply changed their patches and became the Bosnian Serb army under General Ratko Mladic, and that this was still effectively -- as we understood it, effectively controlled from Belgrade with salaries and other supplies coming from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the witness says that he is perfectly familiar with the situation in the former Yugoslavia. So put a question to the witness that concerns what was said in the course of the examination-in-chief, a question that will be of use to you, because to discuss Mr. Clinton's book -- well, that's all very well, but how does this help you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put my question to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Towards the end of October 1992, did Lord Owen and UN negotiator, the former secretary of state, Cyrus Vance, present a plan for the regionalisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? It was submitted to the members for them to make comments on. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know at the beginning of February, President Clinton decided not to support the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The history is more complicated, and here I feel that it's getting really beyond -- not an area related to my direct scope of the -- of my testimony. And so -- but it's more complicated than to say that President Clinton did not support the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Unfortunately I have to draw the conclusion that whenever one starts discussing the framework of the events in the former Yugoslavia unfolded, the assessment of the international community, the embargo on arms, transferring staff to Bosnia and Herzegovina, et cetera, when it comes to that no one wants to discuss these matters because this would open up subjects which are a disgrace for the west, according to Mrs. Thatcher. But we will find an expert, and we will also cover those subjects. I have two questions about eastern Mostar, isolation and shelling. My question is as follows: One of the witnesses, Mr. Beese, in item 76, 130, 134 of his report, reference is constantly made to the Serbian shelling of Mostar. My question is as follows. How far the gun positions, the gun emplacements of the Bosnian Herzegovinian Serbs from Mostar, how far were these positions from Mostar, from the eastern part, from the western part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I just want to comment on your statement because in fact I did discuss the embargo on arms and I did tell you that I thought it was the wrong decision. I thought it was a very wrong decision, and I did discuss the way in which Milosevic transferred troops to -- or changed from the JNA to the Bosnian Serb army and maintained control. So I think it's unfair to say that no one wants to discuss these matters and I've discussed them at great length in other forums. And I don't -- I may not agree on the particulars, but I think I've said very clearly that the international community had a wrong response to the events in Bosnia, and I'm not saying this in 2006. I said so at the time when I was visiting in 1991, 1992. And I worked hard to change the response, which our administration did do, and I think one reason why we got to the peace that now exists. You've asked about item 176 [sic], 130, and 134. I think I would like to see that before I would try to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: 76. I'm afraid I don't know how to find this right now. It was item 76 and it was a Prosecution witness. Would it be sufficient for me to read out what he actually said? Will you trust me on that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no offence, but I feel that if I'm going to be asked about something that is an item that's in the record, I ought to see the item because that really will give me the total understanding of something that I'm asked to respond to. And I think, as I've explained, it's hard to do that when you're reading something in Croatian and then I'm going to try and listen to it in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, do you have the relevant reference that concerns page 176, provided it has a link to the -- or a relation to the questions that were put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 76, 103, and 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That doesn't really help us, Your Honour. And I want to support the Ambassador's concern. If -- he's been very cooperative, but if counsel or the accused wants to put questions to the witness, please have the document shown to him. Now, Mr. Praljak must know if he's done enough preparation to refer to 176, 103, and 104, he must know what document he's referring to. So please let him show us and direct our attention and, more importantly, the witness's attention to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the number of the document, if I can help, was 960 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The number of the document is 9601. I should respect fully remind the Court, before reference is made to that, that Mr. Beese's request it was under seal and was not publicly read. So I ask the Court to bear that in mind if passages are read from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we should move into private session. This document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, did the United Nations, and by the same token the United States of America, proclaim protected areas as Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde, Sarajevo, Bihac, did they proclaim these areas to be protected areas?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: And in the legal sense, did that mean that the countries used to protect those areas will use all their power and authority to protect the lives of the people there and the property, the property of the inhabitants living in those protected areas, would that be their duty?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately it didn't happen that way, and they should have done more. I really can't speak to the legal duty of what countries. I think there was a moral duty on the part of the United Nations to have protected the safe areas. And I think the United Nations, and by that I don't mean the institution in New York but the countries who are its members, failed in that moral duty. I'm not saying, Mr. Praljak, that there was not also a legal duty, it's simply that -- I would have to think about the legal issues involved more than I can right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you.
