I think we all know what actually happened, and it is quite clear that Kiseljak wouldn't have fared better, and I stand by my decision in a set period of time in a set area to proclaim the aggressor the party that is attacking us and not the party that you or the United States of America proclaimed the aggressor. And at that time the aggressor, as far as I was concerned, was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I behaved the way I think I should have behaved. Now, another question, on the 9th of September, 1993, in Grabovica 32 Croats were killed. On the 28th of July, 1993, in Doljani, 63 were killed. On the 14th of September, at Prozor, the casualties were 41. On the 16th of September, 1993, Hudocko, 24 casualties. In Bugojno, after the fall of Bugojno, 118 fatalities. In Travnik in June, 120 persons were killed. And the total number of crimes of Muslims against the Croats in 21 municipalities is 1.184. Now, did you have those facts and figures presented to you when you made your decisions and assessments? Did you have those facts and figures, clear-cut facts and figures when you looked at the psychological, social aspects, the problems that families entailed and looking at the overall population of these fatalities, did you have all these facts and figures when you made your decisions and evaluations of the situation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Praljak, I do not accept that what you've just described are facts. They are, of course, figures. I simply am not in a position to say whether they're correct or not. But we were -- I was aware and heard at great length from the Croatian officials with whom I met of the actions of the Army of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and allegations of atrocities. As I said to President Tudjman and to Defence Minister Susak - and I'll say it to you - the fact that one side may have - - may or may not - and I'm not saying they did - may or may not have committed atrocities, in no way, in the view of the United States, it in no way excused the atrocities committed by the HVO. And that was the message that I delivered very constantly in -- from June 28th, 1993, until the Washington Agreement brought the Muslim-Croat war to an end. That regardless of what happened any place else in Bosnia, we did not accept and we considered it to be a crime, the shelling of civilians in east Mostar, the destruction of cultural property, including the destruction of the old bridge, the denial of food and -- or to starve a population -- that is, the blocking of humanitarian convoys, and the holding of prisoners in inhumane conditions. The fact that others committed crimes -- and I think there's no doubt that -- and this has always been the view of the United States government, there is no doubt that the greatest part of the crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina were committed by the Bosnian Serbs, by the Bosnian Serb army, by -- and the forces under the control of General Ratko Mladic. I mean, I can't give you a figure, but I would suppose it's in the neighbourhood of 80 per cent of the atrocities. Nonetheless, that fact does not in any way excuse or condone, in the view of the United States government at the time that I was Ambassador, the atrocities that were committed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I fully agree, sir. But why is it that in explaining a social phenomenon, death, crimes, retaliation, hate, we resort to the legal formulation? I do not justify that, et cetera, et cetera, and that is not justifiable, et cetera, et cetera. And all reasonable people agree there, but my question to you, sir, is the following: You dealt with politicological analyses and regardless of the justification of something or not, did you ever encounter anywhere that one evil causes evil to be done on the other side, that evil begets evil. In America, retaliation after 9/11 towards the Muslim. In Baghdad, for example, we can see what the control of an army of numbering 200.000 men looks like when something begins called madness, what kind of control you can exert there. So my question to you is as follows, after so much evil, after so many crimes committed, have you ever seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I believe as it was already previously said that you are entering into a pleading and it is not a question. And therefore I would ask you to mainly concentrate on questions which could be asked from Ambassador Galbraith. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for all your guidelines. I will of course abide by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is as follows: In history is there any example, Mr. Galbraith, that you can mention in any war where evil did not beget evil, regardless of the legal aspects? Can you name any example?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a -- as you supposed the question, that's a very hard one to answer. There may be some examples, depending on how you defined your terms. But if your point is that the evil of war leads to other evils --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, but I just wanted to ask you whether you had an example or not, without entering into a debate. Do you have any example of where evil was committed on one side without retaliation on the other side and evil on the other side? You can say you don't know, you can't remember; Praljak's right, Praljak's not right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think Praljak -- well, I think there are -- there are certainly examples where one side committed war crimes and the other side did not, even though they were victims of the crimes. Yes, I think there are plenty of examples of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back now -- but before I do, I have one more question. Let me ask you one question and I'll move on to Franjo Tudjman. In what way and from whom was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina armed throughout the conflict with the HVO? How? By whom? Where? What were the channels and means? Who armed the Bosnia-Herzegovina army?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, although we've been outside the scope of my direct testimony for some time, I can't see that this has really anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, according to the documents that were approved by the United States government, and I've been sitting here reviewing them, I have the list in front of me, and this is not on the list of topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard on this issue because I think this is extremely relevant, this is an extremely relevant point. The gentleman was the Ambassador at the time. He was briefed prior to going into country. Now, he's made certain allegations here, and I think this is an important issue. Obviously he would have known. There's also the issue of whether -- with respect to the embargo. The issue is -- he's not only indicting Praljak, he's also indicting Croatia and Tudjman, and as we have the testimony we know that shipments of arms were going from Croatia into Bosnia. Okay. We know that the United States turned a blind eye. We know that even Iran wanted to bring in and did in fact bring in -- and was bringing in prior to the gentleman's arrival -- so I think these are relevant questions. How can an Ambassador sit there with a pregnant pause of approximately two minutes and not be able to know or answer that question. So I think this is extremely relevant. It goes to the nature of his briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, why is it? We have these assertions that this is extremely important, extremely relevant, why? Why? How is any of that a defence to what the accused are charged with in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who armed the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, how is that possibly relevant to any legal issue in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's relevant, Your Honour, because on the one hand if you are trying to divide this country and if you're trying to slaughter the Muslims, as they would have us believe, then why would you at the same time arm them in order so they can shoot you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because they were fighting the Serbs, Your Honour, that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my opinion, this is pertinent because it arose from the answers given by the Ambassador to the effect that the Croatian army, the HV, was located in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the return of the HV was called for as well as armaments. So there is a context there which is linked to weapons. Now, if the Ambassador does not wish to answer and stand behind what was the subjects approved for discussion, I agree. So, Mr. Ambassador, you've understood what the Defence has asked you. They are asking for clarifications, and it's up to you to decide whether you're going to answer or not. I'm not going to force you to answer, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will answer in general terms. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had weapons that were -- that came from -- weapons that citizens in Bosnia and Herzegovina had. I suppose some weapons that they got from JNA depots, not many, but some that way; from the Bosnian territorial force of the former Yugoslavia. There were some weapons that were smuggled in. There were some weapons that were purchased on the grey market and on the black market. In period 1991 and 1992, there may have been weapons that came from Croatian sources or through Croatia. So far as I can recall, during the Muslim-Croat war, the Bosnian -- the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not getting very many weapons for the simple reason that it was surrounded on the one side by the Bosnian Serb army enemy, and on the other side by Croatia and the HVO. After that war ended, there was a flow of arms that came through Croatia and -- which actually was fairly significant and which enabled the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to survive and then to successfully resist the Bosnian Serbs. And ultimately, that flow of weapons helped turn the tide which made possible the change in the military situation in August of 1995 through September/October, that in turn paved the way to the peace agreement. Now, the issue has been raised of the role of the United States in this. I have testified at great length about it and for congressional committees. I'm very happy to testify again because I think the decision that President Clinton took and that I implemented, which was that we would not object to the flow of weapons through -- from -- through Croatia to Bosnia was a -- the correct decision. The Defence counsel has characterised it as turning a blind eye. I suppose that's one way you could characterise it. It was a correct decision and it was very significant in the fact that the military balance changed and we were able to get to the peace agreement at Dayton. It's a long topic. I'm happy to spend a lot of time talking about it. I'm not sure how relevant it is to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your very comprehensive answer. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, although I asked you the following. The BH army unfortunately did not have that kind of weaponry, but during the Croatian- Muslim conflict which was ongoing, what did the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina used to shoot from and is it true that at those times we allowed ammunition to get through to the BH army for it to shoot? And is it also correct that this is something that has not been recorded in the annals of warfare throughout history. Have never been seen before. You can say you don't know and we'll move on, Mr. Ambassador, to make the best use of your time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me questions to which you know much better the answer than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Say you don't know, then, Mr. Praljak and I'll move on. I'd like to go back to Franjo Tudjman now, just short questions. He was in the Partizans, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: He was one of the youngest generals in Tito's Yugoslav People's Army, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: He dealt with historical research, the results of which were not in conformity of the official version of Yugoslavia at the time, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: He was imprisoned twice, in 1972 and again in 1983. He was convicted to a prison sentence, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: He wrote about ten books, and I'm going to quote from three of them. The national question in contemporary Europe, in modern-day Europe; great ideas, small nations; and the biroads or cul-de-sacs of historical circumstance. Now, have you ever seen any ideas of -- do you know the kind of ideas that Franjo Tudjman puts forward in his books?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly know some of the ideas that Franjo Tudjman put forward in his books.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that a state solution for Bosnia- Herzegovina from the 16th century was also imposed by somebody else by force, the Turks, the Berlin Congress, the -- Austria with the Anschluss, Versailles by creating a single Yugoslavia, Jaulta -- or rather the first Yugoslavia by creating a second Yugoslavia, and finally this brings us to the Washington Accords and Dayton Accords. Were solutions always imposed? Was it ever left to the people living there? Did they ever have the right and possibility of deciding what they're going to do themselves?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I feel I'm being drawn into huge debates which I suppose I would say to you: Why don't you get a historian, not that I'm unfamiliar with the history, but there are certain -- there's -- I mean Bosnia and Herzegovina, like Croatia, and Serbia for that matter, was a small country. It was occupied by foreign powers, part of foreign empires that adopted cultures from those empires. Other people made decisions about them. That was true of Croatia. It's frankly true of lots of different countries. Can I say to you that the people in Bosnia and Herzegovina never made their own decisions? Well, I don't know. I think they've had some say in it. There have been democratic elections there. Was the Dayton Agreement imposed on Bosnia in the same breath as the Ottoman occupation? No, I don't think so. It was a peace treaty made among the parties that ended an absolutely horrific war that cost well more than 100.000 lives, involved many atrocities, which are the subject of the jurisdiction of this terrific court. And -- but it was something that certainly the international community and particularly my country encouraged, did everything in our power to bring about, but I also think that the -- all the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina concluded that the peace agreement, however imperfect, was better than the alternative of a continued war. And I don't think that -- I think that it's impossible for anybody to argue anything different, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I, of course, would present different arguments and state that a bad agreement leads to bad consequences. But when it comes to the Dayton Agreement, is it true and correct that the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina have a republic, a constitution, laws, a parliament, territory, television, they can use their own language, and does the -- do the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina have any of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to relevance, Your Honour. One, completely beyond the scope of direct examination; completely beyond the scope of the rule set by the United States government; and three, completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Mr. Scott. You are dealing with a period after the facts. It might be interesting from the point of view of politics or history; however, the field of testimony of the Ambassador does not include the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the gentleman did mention Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but the witness said on page 36 of the transcript it says, line 13 to 15, that he was proud of what his country's diplomacy managed to do. The diplomacy of his country did take part in the Dayton Agreements, it created the Dayton Agreements. So I think to discuss and elaborate on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in connection with the Dayton Agreements does follow on from the testimony made by this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to go from that comment, a broad comment by the Ambassador, rightly said that he was proud of bringing peace, being part of bringing peace to the country is a far cry from whether they have televisions in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard, Mr. President, very briefly and perhaps this gentleman is not the best witness for this. The issue is relevant because whatever the Republika Srpska has as an entity within Bosnia-Herzegovina as a result of the Dayton Peace Accords, if we look at the peace processes from 1991 onwards, that was on the table more or less at the -- from the very beginning. And so -- and then to go full swing back into Dayton. But again, this gentleman may not be the best individual. But I think it is relevant to the extent of whether he knew of the different proposals that were on the table. Because we see from the Dayton Accords what you have is two entities within a government and plus a district, the Brcko district, which they have their own constitution, all within the framework of the then-existing constitution of BiH, which is something that the Croats were striving throughout this period. Again, this might not be the best witness for this, but I can understand the relevancy to Mr. Praljak's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to Mr. Karnavas's speeches and assertions of evidence. There is no evidence that any of this is true. There is no evidence that any of these people -- leadership of Herceg-Bosna was supporting the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina during this time. So for Mr. Karnavas to get up and make these assertions does not mean it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I direct the Trial Chamber to the testimony of Mr. Kljujic as we walk through the process of the various peace accords and I don't want to get into a debate since we have a witness here. But I suggest that perhaps better attention be paid to the testimony as it comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a certain relevance, but the witness is perhaps not the most appropriate person to discuss such a subject, as the Chamber has granted Mr. Praljak an hour and a half and time is running out. I believe that Mr. Praljak should ask questions that are of importance. Try and focus your questions on your particular case, on your personal case, rather than on the Dayton Agreement. That will certainly be referred to again, but try to focus your questions. This is in your own interest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I personally don't have a problem with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you have used up an hour and 16 minutes, of -- which means that you have another 24 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll take less than that. To repeat what I said, I don't have any personal problems. And to my mind, this gentleman didn't say anything that would incriminate me and I don't think that his impressions and conclusions are well-grounded and documents, and this became evident through this examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is: The treaties that changed from month to month as it pleased a country that was in charge of it, be it France or the United States, all these peace agreements, were they not first signed by the president of the Croatian state, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, the politician, wasn't he the first one to sign each of them? Can you give us any exceptions to this? Wasn't he the first one to sign each and every peace agreement? And this pertains to the political wing of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly give you exceptions to the notion that Franjo Tudjman signed all the peace agreement that the international mediators put on the table, starting with the Z-four plan which was sponsored by the United States, United Nations, Russia, and the European Union, and he was also extremely reluctant about the Washington Agreement, although eventually he did agree to it. In other cases he was -- he did sign on to some of the international plans, either because he found that -- found them to be advantageous to the Bosnian Croat population or because he thought that the others weren't going to sign and so that he could have some benefit from signing on. Incidentally, the phrase "signing" I don't think would be correct because I don't recall that any of these were documents that were signed because they were not agreed to, so many of the different peace plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: They were not agreed to because at least two and always one side failed to sign these peace agreements. Now, when you mentioned the Z-four plan, it envisaged full state autonomy for the Serbs in Krajina, the constitution, government, currency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it envisioned full state autonomy, but it would have given the -- the Serb majority part of the Krajina region substantial self-government within a unified Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: With money, currency, and government?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have had their own government, just like American states do and Swiss cantons, and many others in those kinds of systems. They would not, let me emphasise, they would not have had their own money. The money of that region would have been the Croatian kuna. They could, however, have had their own bank notes with their own design on them, just as Scotland has the Scottish pound, which is a monetary unit that is the same as the English pound but it has a Scottish design on it. That is the sole issue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: When Franjo Tudjman objected to the Washington Agreement in which you said you'll enter into federation with the Muslims occupying 49 per cent of the territory and then you'll join Croatia in a confederation. When he as a statesman challenged it, you took it against him because he wasn't humble enough, because he put up some minor objection. Any declaration on human rights and rights of citizens starting with the English one or the French one, what gives you the right to take this position and what makes you believe that nobody has the right to object to it without being declared a criminal? Where do you find legal support for such a position?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now tell you that the Serb nation in Croatia are an ethnic minority, and the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina are a constituent nation. I just wanted to supplement my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow the witness to answer the question. Ambassador Galbraith, could you answer the question? Are you capable of answering the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I served five years in this part of the world, so I think I can handle almost any question. I'm just trying to understand it. The -- the first point is the United States was actually reluctant to become involved in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. And Croatia -- and President Tudjman was desperate for our involvement. So it's not as if we imposed ourselves; on the contrary, he basically begged for our involvement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: Except for the embargo.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really discussing the events from the time I was the Ambassador, but it's true that even before then he was seeking American involvement, American support, and above all American involvement in the peace process. As a matter of fact, the so-called Z-four process began as a Russian initiative and on the plane back from Washington, the signing of the Washington Agreement, I flew on President Tudjman's plane -- sorry, it was on the way to Washington, actually, he asked for me to become involved in that process as a co-sponsor. Now, obviously when the United States is brought into something -- and we were invited in -- asked by the president of Croatia to do that. We agreed to do that. It was part of the, if you will, the way in which our relations improved precisely because he signed the Washington Agreement. But when we get involved we obviously are going to do as we see best like any good peace mediator to try and bring about a peaceful solution. And that's of course exactly what we -- what we did. With regard to the Washington Agreement, President Tudjman resisted the idea for a long time, but he ultimately - and I believe reluctantly - but he did ultimately accept it and enter into it. But before he entered into the Bosnian -- into the Washington Agreement, he clearly had aspirations for annexing to Croatia the Croat territory and, for that matter, Muslim -- a Bosniak-majority territory into Croatia. And even afterwards, these dreams did not die. He kept pulling out maps that would show a territory that, in his view, should become part of a Greater Croatia. And he kept insisting that Bosnia and Herzegovina would not survive as a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I believe that your time has run out. Mr. Registrar, could you tell me how much time Mr. Praljak has left at his disposal because there are other Defence teams that need to take the floor. And, as you know, tomorrow we will be adjourning at 1.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used up an hour and 26 minutes, which leaves you with four minutes. Use your four minutes to go to the crux of the matter. Unfortunately your lawyer will not have any time to put questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, we agreed on the division of time among the Defence counsel. So in addition to the hour and a half that you adopt -- that you allotted to Mr. Praljak, we have an additional 60 minutes. So Mr. Praljak plans to leave some time for me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have three more minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the 60 additional minutes, who has allocated this time to you? Mr. Kovacic, who has given you an additional hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. We were given 20 minutes by the Defence of the accused Coric, and the entire time allotted to the Defence of Mr. Pusic. And I thank them for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I wasn't aware of that. We have four minutes before the break. Please go ahead, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P6251 which is the transcript of the 29th of October, 1993, or records, minutes from that meeting. We need to see page 2 in the Croatian version. Next page, please. Next one, please. This one, yes. Can we see the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: I can read it out to you to save time. Mr. Wirth says four lines from the top: "As to what's going to happen in the central -- in central and eastern Europe, it never even occurred to us that something of this nature would happen. I don't think that it occurred to anyone else." And then Dr. Franjo Tudjman says: "In his -- in my book 'National question and contemporary Europe' I anticipated that multi-ethnic states cannot exist -- cannot continue to exist in Europe and that the unification of Europe is only possible in the forum of Europe representing the United States of Europe."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... page 3, it would be probably good to have the witness to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we see the English version of this document on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm told that we have a technical problem, which means that we can't see the English version of the document on the screen. Put your question to the witness. You have translated this or you have had it translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PRALJAK
utterances.text: My question is: As you stated in Globus, the Croatian weekly on the 1st of September, 1996, did you learn the following in Croatia. I'm quoting. "Once you establish democracy, you cannot make the people live in that state against their will. This is the lesson I learned in Croatia." Did I quote your words right and did you apply the logic of the break-up in the upcoming break-up of Iraq as you stated in your book? Thank you for putting up with me, Mr. Galbraith. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, you have finished your testimony with a theatrical touch. I'm going to have to get that quote, which is of course one that I have used frequently to describe the situation in Iraq and the inevitability of an independent Kurdistan. And I say those words frequently these days. I didn't realise I said them as long ago as the 1st of October, 1996. So thank you for calling that to my attention, and I did say that and it is a -- I do say that it is a lesson that I learned from my experience in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, kindly. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for some awkwardness in my examination. I think the topic is such that we cannot limit ourselves to simple questions because this witness spoke of conclusions not only of facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 20 to 6.00 now. We'll have the break that we have to have, the 20-minute break. And we will then have another hour. I believe that Mr. Kovacic will be taking the floor after the break, and then tomorrow the other Defence teams will take the floor and we will adjourn tomorrow at 1.45 p.m. We will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor for an hour now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Ambassador. I'm the Defence counsel of the accused Mr. Praljak. My name is Bozidar Kovacic, I am an attorney-at-law from Rijeka. I will be putting questions to you in Croatian because that's easier for me. You've already testified twice, so you are familiar with the procedure. We have to make breaks between questions and answers and I don't think you will find this to be a problem. You said when you started testifying that you were the US Ambassador in Zagreb, and as such you -- over a long period of time, and you got to know the situation quite well during that turbulent period of time. And I have no doubt that you have first-hand information about certain facts that I have ask you about. Is it true that the Republic of Croatia recognised the sovereign Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 7th of April, 1992, and that it was the practically first state to recognise the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina after its independence was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia certainly was very quick in recognising Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Unconditionally, right? It was a case of direct recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state, one of the former republics of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: General recognition is unconditional, but the Croatian recognition was unconditional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the moment of the recognition they proceeded to establish diplomatic relations between the two countries at the formal level, which also included the opening of the BH embassy in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Among the Zagreb Corps Diplomatique you must have known that in May or June of 1992 an ambassador came from Sarajevo, a lady ambassador, and that the embassy remained open all the way until the Dayton Accords, similar to all other embassies.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The embassy remains open until this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you. Is it true that the Republic of Croatia as a state during the conflict between Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina never attempted to break the diplomatic relations or limit the diplomatic work in any way, the diplomatic functioning of the BH embassy in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia certainly never broke diplomatic relations with Bosnia. I can't speak to any restrictions that might have been placed on the Bosnian embassy, but I can say that I was not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, do you know that soon after the BH embassy was open in Zagreb, this embassy was given an approval from the Government of the Republic of Croatia that they had sought to open two offices within the embassy, one housed the military and economic office, and the other one was the logistics office of the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the BH in Zagreb. Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall all the details, but I know that there was a military attache from Bosnia and Herzegovina and that a part of the embassy did deal with economic affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to now ask for the record 3D00186 which is a document marked for identification for the time being. I would like to put it to the Ambassador because he does seem to have some recollections about it. So perhaps this could further refresh his memory. Could we see 3D00186, please. Mr. Ambassador, they're going to put on the screen this document. The English version will be on the left, the Croatian on the right. This is a letter, this is not in the typical form of a diplomatic note, but perhaps we could call it a note of the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb. The date is the 16th of July, 1993, at least this is when it was received at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Croatia. And here they ask for this approval, for this permission. Would you please look at the two paragraphs which are right above the lists of names. It says here that the following persons work in the military and economic office, and then follows the list of six names. And then there is the list of people working in the logistics office of the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of BH in Zagreb. The list continues on to the next page. Could we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then they also list another group and then they say that in Split in the logistics office of the staff of the Supreme Command the following persons are employed. Mr. Ambassador, my question is as follows. Given the state of affairs, and this is taking place in the summer of 1993, at that time the conflict between Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims was in progress in Bosnia and Herzegovina. As you told us, Franjo Tudjman and his people or cabinet ministers were in full control. According to you, they were the real masters of the actions of the HVO in Bosnia and Herzegovina. How can we reconcile this contradiction that simultaneously, Croatia according to your view and the view of others wanted to position itself as the lord, as the master of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina on one hand and then on the other hand allow that same country, Bosnia and Herzegovina, to open its offices in Zagreb. What's more, the logistics office of the staff of the Supreme Command of armed forces, not only did they have 21 persons employed in Zagreb but also two persons in the branch office in Split. Isn't this unprecedented in war for one warring party to allow the other warring party to have such freedom in its territory? Maybe I exaggerated a bit. I apologise. My first question is this: Since you had some information about this, do you believe this to be true, what stems from this document?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt that the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina submitted this diplomatic note that you show here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question, as I have already said, can you provide us with an explanation as to why Croatia allowed a foreign country, a country that it was at war with, to act within Croatia and in Zagreb in an unrestricted way? Has this ever been recorded in contemporary history?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I think this is a very important point. Since international armed conflict is an issue in this case, do I understand counsel's question to indicate, to concede and to confirm that in fact there was a war going on between the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the state of the Republic of Croatia? That's what he just asserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not my admission that's the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 76, line 19: "Provide us with an explanation as to why Croatia allowed a foreign country, a country that it was at war with" sounds like an international war to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is within the framework of the indictment, and the statements that this witness has commented on. The witness in fact said on a number of occasions that Croatia had total control over the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: If I may, I -- it seems to be a little piece of flippancy on Mr. Scott's part which we can no doubt excuse, but clearly Mr. Kovacic is asking a question why, on the assumption if there is a war going on, would Croatia act in this way. I think that's the obvious sense of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very brief question that I'd like to put. It should have been asked but it wasn't. There is a document that shows there was an embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb and there was an Ambassador. Did you ever meet this Ambassador because ambassadors usually meet each other, at least when there are national holidays. Did you ever meet this person on the 4th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspect I met Ambassador Turkovic on the 4th of July. She probably came to our July 4th party, but I also met her on many other occasions because she solicited our help in trying to secure access for humanitarian convoys and also in dealing with various problems of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether in that embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb there were 19 -- 99 per cent of the staff of 100 per cent of the staff were employees of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and they were all Muslims by nationality? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that I know who all the staff were of the Bosnian embassy. I'm not surprised that they were all Bosnian, and I suppose I would have expected that the very large number of them would have ended up being Muslims. I think I should point out that this is a diplomatic note from the embassy of Bosnia to the Croatian foreign ministry. What is missing here is a response from the Croatian foreign ministry that in fact grants these people permission to operate in Croatia. Perhaps that was granted, but it's -- it wouldn't be immediately clear to me looking at this document that in fact the Croatian government did grant the permission or at what time they granted the permission. And then frankly beyond that, even if they had granted the permission, there would be a separate process by which they would have to get accredited or approved. And so the fact that the request was made doesn't mean that the Croatian government in fact allowed these people actually to begin to operate out of the embassy. I simply don't know the answer, but this document isn't proof that that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ambassador Galbraith, I fully agree with what you have just said, but there are two facts. If I haven't misunderstood what you said, you said that you knew that there was an embassy in existence and that there were -- well, in any event, I'm sure that you said that the embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in existence and was operational in Zagreb. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I certainly was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that. Ambassador, I do agree with your comment as to -- as to whether this -- these individuals actually worked. I don't want to go into technical details. Believe me, though, there is a large amount of evidence that shows that the people mentioned in this document were proved and they did actually work in Zagreb. But I won't ask you any other questions about this. We can deal with this matter with other witnesses. You could be of far greater use to us when it comes to certain other subjects, but thank you for your comment. You also mentioned the fact that Croatian -- that Croatia paid HVO soldiers and provided the HVO budget. I think that that was -- just a minute. I can't find the number of the page, but do you agree that that is more or less what you said?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that Croatia funded the HVO and provided for the budget, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. To be quite clear about everything, to put our cards on the table, could we have the following document on the screen 3D00299. Ambassador Galbraith, you will now see a letter on the screen from the office of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb. It's one of the bodies that the embassy is asking about. It wants authorisation for its operations. This is before 1994, but in the -- in January 1993, as early as January 1993, the military delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia asked the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia - and I'm skipping certain parts and skipping the courteous comments at the beginning - they requested that in order to improve the expert work and organisation and for the sake of higher efficiency in the conflict against the Serbian Chetnik aggressor and for the needs of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, offices of the HV should be allowed to operate. And then there are three names. There's the colonel who operates in the area of Rijeka-Gospic, there's this major in Dubrovnik, et cetera, and then they request that the status of these offices be resolved, as has been the case to date. By putting the status on hold, and then in brackets (in order to have all the authority of Croatian army officers), that means that they should have a salary and medical coverage, et cetera. It also requests that after they have carried out their tasks, that means their tasks in Bosnia, they should be allowed to be further engaged in the HV. And then gratitude is expressed and Colonel Hasan Efendic signed the letter. This letter was drafted, as you can see at the top of the letter, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this is an example, and we can assume on the basis of the text that there are other examples, that the ABiH is in fact asking the Ministry of Defence in Croatia to lend them a number of individuals. They needed them. There were -- they were people who had been trained in the military. They should be allowed to go to Bosnia, to the ABiH, to carry out the tasks that were needed within the context of the fight against the Chetniks. They should then be allowed to return having carried out their tasks. In the meantime, they requested that they pay their salaries and other benefits, and this request was made in January 1993. At the time, it's true that a full-blown conflict between the Croats and the Muslims hadn't broken out in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the situation was tense and there had been certain incidents. Does this seem quite normal to you? If there really is a conflict between those two countries or if it's obvious that such a conflict could break out at any point in time, and that was quite obvious at the time, is it normal for Croatia in such case to cooperate in military terms by providing soldiers of their own? They are Muslims; we can see that on the basis of their names, but they are members of the Croatian army who live in Croatia. Is this a normal and logical way in which to act?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first point I would make is, once again, this is the request from the military delegation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we do not -- you haven't showed me the answer. So I can't say whether in fact the Republic of Croatia agreed to this request. And just to put it in context with your previous comment, of course it is perfectly normal and legitimate for the internationally recognised government operating through its embassy to make such a request for foreign military officers to come and serve or even serve in their own army. That, of course, is quite different from sending in your army without the permission of the sovereign government or sending generals and officers and troops of your army to go to be part of the army of an irregular and not- legitimate military force of a foreign country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I can't accept your, let me call it hypothetical analysis, but let's not discuss whether these people were actually given permission to do this or not. But let's approach this in a hypothetical way. If they were sent there, in that case I would claim that similarly members of the Croatian people who lived in Croatia went to Bosnia and Herzegovina as volunteers, to defend their homeland you mentioned, the late Gojko Susak who was from that area. His ancestors s were from that area and he had intended to return there when he retired. And why would that be negative if people went to a country they came from? You're familiar with Croatian history, with Yugoslav history. You know people were free to move around that country. They would leave Bosnia and Herzegovina and go to Croatia for the purposes of education or find work there. So my thesis according to which there was a fluctuation or movement of people, both Croats and Muslims moved around. And some people went back to the territory they originally came from to defend their homeland. Would you agree with this thesis of mine?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say for citizens of one country to go on to the territory of another country as volunteers to fight in a militia or non-legal armed force is illegal and that the sending country has an obligation to prevent it. I would say that the obligation to prevent it is even higher when the sending country sends its own troops to go be the troops in this militia or illegal force, and perhaps the burden is even the greatest when the sending country sends a general in the army of the sending country to go be the commanding general of the -- in a -- of an irregular force that is not accepted and not under the authority of the government of the -- of the country to which the person is being sent. So in short, I think the -- the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose embassy was in Zagreb, could have legitimately requested any Croatian army officer to come serve, including -- could have made a request for somebody to come serve and be the commanding general. And if Croatia wanted to do that, that was fine. But what was not appropriate was, in my view, was for the Government of Croatia to send somebody without the approval of the Government of Croatia [as interpreted]to a non-recognised armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure we should continue with this discussion because there is one thing that is a fact. I'll nevertheless ask you a question about this. These people, these inhabitants of the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and the inhabitants of Croatia within the former Yugoslavia suddenly found themselves in a new situation. All of a sudden in 1992 the village -- or part of the village was divided by a state border, and then one inhabitant or some of the inhabitants, regardless of whether they were Muslims or Croats, and let's forget about the legality of such acts, decided to go home to defend his village. It's quite simple, according to the most contemporary standards of human rights. Could we deny the person who was from the other side of the village the right to return home and to defend his village, especially if that person was aware of the fact that no one would defend him? We are speaking about the beginning of the conflict. We are speaking about the time when the Serbs started taking territory and they soon had two-thirds. We are talking about the time when Izetbegovic said: This isn't our war. That was when the JNA took Ravno, et cetera, you know what I'm speaking about. So these -- is this situation the same as the situation in which Mexico might send its army to another country? You'll have to agree that that is not the case. The facts are quite different. We can't look at this in formalistic or legal manner, not within the context of the events that actually happened on the ground. Will you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, before it leaves the page there's an error in the transcript on page 83, line 17, it says the approval of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, not the Government of Croatia. And, Your Honour, at this time I'm also going to object to these long comments that are -- tend to be presented as questions but they're -- look at the transcript right now. Mr. Kovacic has made a long speech that there's really no -- there's really no question and then at the end a nominal question. These are just arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps the question might appear a rather lengthy one, I agree with that, but let me say two things. Ambassador Galbraith is not the ordinary type of witness which demands classical questions in the usual way, but I have put my question at the end of a lengthy presentation. But I nevertheless would like to ask the Ambassador to answer my question because it was a clear question in the end. Are they rather circumstances -- or rather, you could pass through the village until yesterday with a uniform and your weapon and now suddenly you weren't allowed to do that. We're talking about ordinary people, ordinary inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with that, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have sympathy with the point that you're making. I would say, however, that one of the consequences of no longer being Yugoslavia and having independent states is that the successor states had obligations and -- just as the United States has an obligation to prevent -- well, to take an actual example, Cuban Americas, that is people who came from Cuba but are citizens of the United States, taking up arms and fighting against the government of Cuba, and we do try to prevent that even though we have a hostile relationship with Cuba. So nonetheless there would be an effort to prevent citizens from going across a border and fighting in an irregular force without the permission and approval of the government of that country. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- go on to say that, again, in the circumstances of war that existed when all these events unfolded in 1991 and 1992, I do have some sympathy with the real situation on the ground. But I would say that that -- even that situation that you describe is of course totally different from taking an officer -- a year later, an officer or the -- a general from the Croatian army and sending him to be the commander of an irregular force that is -- a military force that is not the lawful armed forces of the country without the permission of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand, yes. Now back to that same topic, two short questions. Do you know that -- are you aware of the fact that in 1992 and 1993 there were arguments in existence between Izetbegovic and Tudjman on cooperation which in fact did allow this kind of conduct? And the request I that I showed you earlier on was based on that. It allowed people to cross the border to fight the Serbs. You're well-versed in the topic and I'm sure you can confirm the existence of such agreements which were the sort of legal groundwork for that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well there certainly were agreements for military cooperation between Croatia and the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I cannot -- I mean, I would -- before I answer in these general terms I would want to look at the different agreements and see exactly as to what they said, but I -- to repeat what I said to you, if it is done -- if the action follows the -- in all regards the lawful request of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it would, in my view, be appropriate. After all, countries are entitled to form alliances, and that is a common and lawful thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Ambassador, do you also know that Alija Izetbegovic said several times publicly that the HVO was a component - and we have a legal regulation about that - but the HVO was a component of the armed forces of the BH army, that's the first point? And secondly, and I'm sure you're aware of this, de facto the HVO, for example, took part in the defence of Sarajevo, together with a Bosnia and Herzegovina army? I'm sure you're well aware of that and can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cooperation between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO at a certain point in time doesn't mean that that is lawful in circumstances where the irregular forces fighting against the lawful army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was the circumstances in 1993. And it does not mean that a foreign country has the right to send its army into the -- on to the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or to send officers in its army to go be commanders of the irregular force or the force that is not the lawful army of the country without the consent of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to that in due course, but I'd like to continue with my set of questions. And I refer to them as facts which are in contradiction with certain views of the relationships that existed between the states at that time. Now, at the beginning of your testimony you said quite clearly that Croatia did take care of refugees from Bosnia- Herzegovina and that it took in a large number of refugees if we look at the total per capita. So quite certainly you have taken a position on that point, and that is realistic and it is what we are claiming all the time. But speaking about the visits by your people to the island of Obonjan and the refugee camp in Gasinci and both of these institutions are on the territory of Croatia, and you spoke about this within the context of the release of persons from the Heliodrom to third countries. For the record, that was on page 64 of yesterday's transcript, lines 24 -- or rather, line 24, and then on page 65, line 9, and then once again on page 80, lines 5 to 16. And in that connection we saw an exhibit P9502. And my question in that regard, I hope I've managed to refresh your memory, that you know what I'm referring to. Do you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you could ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I just had to take you to the relevant portion. My question is as follows. The Republic of Croatia took part in the transfer of refugees to third countries, but in cooperation with the UNHCR and those third countries which accepted those refugees; right?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly Croatia was a place where people came as refugees, and they were taken care of by the Croatian authorities in cooperation with the UNHCR. And a number of them or quite a large number of them went on to third-country re-settlement, including in fact the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that material time, that is to say in October 1992 -- or let me rephrase that and start again. I'm sure you'll be able to confirm that in fact all the humanitarian aid, except for a negligible portion brought in on planes from Sarajevo, that all the humanitarian aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina from the beginning of the Serb aggression right up to the Dayton Accords went through exclusively, exclusively went through the Republic of Croatia, that is to say the transport routes for humanitarian aid went by Croatia, at least from the port of Ploce to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, passing by many ports and airports. Is that true? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be -- yes, that would be substantially correct. I think the air-lift into Sarajevo was not insignificant. I mean, it was very important, but overwhelming the humanitarian assistance that came to Bosnia came through Croatia. It was -- without Croatia, Bosnia would not have survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think that it is quite clear - and please confirm that - that Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, on its own territory never, not at any single point in time, stopped any humanitarian aid convoys going to Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Merhamet, the Muslim charity, that was also one of the participants in that humanitarian aid, worked quite freely in Zagreb and in Croatia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is basically correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We took note a moment ago of refugees or we discussed refugees. Now, do you agree that despite of the heavy burdens on Croatia it never throughout that war stopped or closed the borders, I mean closed the borders and stopped the flow of refugees and said: That's enough. We'll negotiate first and then we'll let the refugees through. So in your talks -- or rather, let me separate those two things. Do we agree that Croatia never closed its borders to refugees coming in from Bosnia- Herzegovina into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is that Croatia had an extraordinarily good record on refugees. It -- I cannot think of another country in the world that took as many refugees in such a short period of time relative to its own population. And generally, the borders were open. I can't say that there was never a moment when they didn't try to stop the flow because this was a matter of concern from time to time -- it was a matter of great concern for the Croatian government and occasionally for the international community. But the fact is that Croatia's record was -- was superb. And this was a very important factor in our policy toward Croatia. Certainly it was one major reason that we were reluctant to go ahead with sanctions at the period of time that I'm discussing because of the consequences that it would have had for -- potential consequences for the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, staying with that topic, refugees, we've all read -- I don't know how many there are, but several hundred records or minutes from the late President Tudjman's office. To make things simpler -- or rather, to ask a question -- I'm going to make an assertion and you can challenge it or not. My team and I did not find a single record in the presidential offices, and you were there fairly often, which states when political issues were dealt with, when agreements were negotiated, Croatia wants this, Izetbegovic wants that, we found no evidence of President Tudjman or any of his associates ever mentioning the possibility of closing off the borders to refugees, that that would be a weapon, a lever, to wield for the negotiations. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What's the question? What's the question, whether Mr. Galbraith, Ambassador Galbraith, agrees that the representation that my team and I did not find a single record. To agree with Mr. -- to agree with the fact or to agree with Mr. Kovacic? What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I apologise if my learned colleague failed to understand me, but my question was simple. That is my assertion that Tudjman made no mention ever of using refugees as leverage in negotiations and I'm asking the Ambassador whether he could confirm or refute that. That's very simple. I know that it's a difficult question for the Prosecution, but that is no reason --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you could have approached the question in a different way. I'm going to ask him, and if I take the time to ask him, it will be your time. When you had discussions with Mr. Tudjman about the question of refugees, on Mr. Tudjman's part and his associates, people around him, was there any reticence with respect to refugees comes in from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia and to go on to third countries? Was there any hesitation on his part? Did you feel him hesitate? Or did he express the will to facilitate this flow of refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first to answer -- well, if I may. First to address the point that the Defence attorney made, which is that in my -- to address his point. In my experience, President Tudjman never used the -- tried to use the refugees as a lever in any of these negotiations. It was not -- it was -- he never responded but, for example, by threatening to cut off the flow. So -- and I think that is an important point. Nor did any other Croatian official try to use that as leverage. To answer your question, Your Honour, there was at times reticence and concern about the flow of refugees because the numbers were so enormous relative to the population of Croatia. And of course the international community provided significant assistance, but it still remained a significant burden on the host country. So I think there was some natural concern expressed from time to time about this -- about this problem. But that statement that there was some concern - and maybe at some time some reticence - doesn't change my overall assessment that the record of Croatia, in terms of receiving refugees, was superb. There were from time to time some problems including -- probably the most serious was the involuntary repatriation to Bosnia of certain refugees, and that was a significant problem that we raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a few short questions, staying on the same topic. Do you agree that Croatia also gave enormous assistance in view of its population in medicines and paid attention not only refugees but to the injured and wounded who were transferred from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatian hospitals, injured persons regardless of their ethnic -- ethnicity and to which army they belonged. And there was public information to that effect I'm sure. Would that be correct? Let me remind you of the Split hospital, the hospital in Slavonski Brod, in Zagreb, Karlovac, and so on.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited many -- some of these hospitals, and Croatia did a very good job of taking care of victims of the -- of the war in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Might I add with no segregation with respect to ethnicity. Were you able to see that for yourself?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that Bosniaks, that is, Muslims, were also treated in these hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, I still have seven or eight minutes left. Do you agree -- or rather, do you know, are you familiar with the fact that the Republic of Croatia also during that period of time, 1992 to 1994, did not undertake any legal sanctions in order to sequester property owned by physical and legal persons who were citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on Croatian territory, that they were free to dispose of their property, their bank accounts and all other property?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that statement is generally correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me return for just a brief moment to something I mentioned earlier on. I need to add an explanation. I mentioned agreements --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the record we tendered the book used by Mr. Praljak. It was 3D00320, that was the number 00320, but it still has the MFI identification on page 343, there's an agreement there, Mr. Ambassador, and it is entitled the agreement between the BH army and the HVO on a cease-fire between the HVO and the BH army. It says: Zenica, the 21st of April, 1993, is the date. I'm sure you'll remember that agreement. It was one of the more important ones, and I'd just like to confirm one thing, something I said earlier on. In point 1, paragraph 1, it says: The BH army and the HVO are legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and are treated equally. That agreement was signed by Sefer Halilovic for the BH army and Milivoj Petkovic on behalf of the Main Staff, Croatian Main Staff, and Philippe Morillon and the head of the observer mission also signed it at the ECMM in Zenica, Ambassador Jean Pierre Thebault. This is not something that you haven't seen before, it's not new to you. Is that declaration correct, do you remember it, do you remember this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agreement was actually before I arrived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that it was before that. But you said you had been briefed about the situation in Bosnia, and this did factor into that period and the developments during that period. You knew the situation.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't now remember what details I was briefed about at the time. Again, I'm not sure that this gives the -- gave Croatia the right to send its army officers to go be the officers of the HVO or to send its army into Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think you were quite clear on that point. You said that clearly on several occasions. I have time for just one more question I believe. Another argument which shows how contradictory the situation was. During your sojourn in Zagreb, did you learn or hear anything about the fact that the Republic of Croatia financed the preparations and travels of Bosnian sportsmen to attend the Olympic games in Albertville in 1992 and to the Mediterranean games in France in 1993. There was a lot about that in the press. Do you happen to remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first was before I arrived in Zagreb. I do recall the international effort to get athletes to the games in 1994 in Lillehammer, Norway. I don't know recall in that connection, however, any particular Croatian effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. May we just have an e-court the following document. P3112. It is a record from Dr. Tudjman's office used by the Prosecution. But until that comes up on our screens let me tell you that it is a meeting that took place on the 2nd of July, 1993, in the office of the late Dr. Tudjman. The counsel for defence and national security of the Republic of Croatia, highly placed officials. May we have the next page, please, I only know the ERN number and it is 01866500. So the last three digits are 500 of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, let me say that Mr. Anton Vrdoljak took the floor. I think you knew him. He was quite a prominent personage in the sphere of sports, et cetera. I'm sure you knew him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: He was also the director of Croatian Radio Television for a time. I'm sure you're remember that as well?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was a member of the -- or rather, president of the Olympic committee of Croatia and today he is a member of the International Olympics Committee?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I knew it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But anyway -- and we have it up on our screens now. I'm reading the last portion from this excerpt where we see what Mr. Vrdoljak. I'm sorry we don't have the English version on our screens. It's 7.00, we're not going to have time, but I'll read it out to you, Mr. Ambassador, just one sentence. "The tragedy lies in the fact that we paid for all their preparations from the Olympics to the European championships for that national team, and here in Zagreb, they trained here in Zagreb, and now their junior team is in Istria is preparing in Istria."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in English it's: "It's tragic that we paid, et cetera -- [In English] "It's tragic that we paid, all the preparations," et cetera. [Interpretation] Not to lose any more time. The president says: "At our expense." And Anton Vrdoljak says: "Yes, at our expense." And the president says: "And you're paying for that," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, does that show once again that Croatia was trying to help Bosnia and Herzegovina on an international level as well because international sports are nothing more than political propaganda. So does that seem to you to be quite normal and usual at a time when allegedly the two parties were at war? And this is July 1993, that Croatia is financing athletes to attend international championships. Doesn't that seem what strange to you, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't see the entire context, but it would seem that Mr. Tudjman is slightly unhappy to learn that Croatian money had been used to finance the Bosnian team. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that that is an answer, too, but I'm just quoting this for the fact as it stands. The fact of the matter.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to answer your question, which I think you yourself stated that the situation was complicated. There is no doubt that Croatia provided assistance to Bosnia-Herzegovina at various times, that it was the first country to recognise it. And even during the Muslim-Croat war there was a -- the Bosnian embassy operated. There was a degree of civility between Bosnian officials and Croatian officials. And I think one of the things that led us to believe that this war could be ended was to see a television show with -- with Muhamed Sacirbey, the Bosnian embassador to the United Nations and Mario Nobilo, the Croatian Ambassador. This was the worst time -- and I think the Yugoslav Ambassador was there. But the two, the Bosnian and the Croatian Ambassadors were friendly to each other and they were stressing the importance of ending this war. And incidentally that was a view that was shared by I think a great majority of the people in Croatia who were deeply appalled by the Muslim-Croat war and who -- I think a majority of whom did not like the idea of Greater Croatia or annexing territory in Herzegovina. All that being said, President Tudjman did have the ambition for a Greater Croatia and he did support military activity by the HVO that was intended to accomplish that goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This -- the continuation of that is that he died in a traffic accident. Drazen Petrovic, Croatia's best basket ballplayer died in an accident and then the national team and Franjo Tudjman was reacting to those vulgar writings about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'd like to thank my client for adding that. I don't think we needed to describe the whole scene and what followed, but anyway that's why I put it on the ELMO, on the overhead projector. Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Ambassador, on behalf of my client and in my own name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is now five minutes past 7.00. The cross-examination will be continued tomorrow. There are a number of Defence counsel who wish to cross-examine, so divide the time amongst yourselves. We will have to conclude by 1.45. Thank you. We adjourn for the day and reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.
